claims.text: A relative path names nothing on its own; the operating system completes it with the working directory of the process that asked.
claims.source_hint: Linux man-pages, path_resolution(7): resolution of a pathname not starting with '/' begins at the process's current working directory

claims.text: An absolute path starts at the top of the file tree, which on Linux is written '/', and names the same file whatever the working directory of the process is.
claims.source_hint: Linux man-pages, path_resolution(7): pathname starting with '/' is resolved from the root directory

claims.text: Every process has a working directory, and it can change while the process is running.
claims.source_hint: Linux man-pages, chdir(2) and getcwd(3): the per-process current working directory and how it is changed

claims.text: A process's working directory is independent of the directory that holds the executable file; the two can differ.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.Environment.CurrentDirectory and System.AppContext.BaseDirectory (Remarks contrasting the two)

claims.text: A file or a folder records an owning user and an owning group, plus read, write and execute permissions held separately for the owner, for the group and for others.
claims.source_hint: Linux man-pages, inode(7) 'The file type and mode' and chmod(2) file mode bits

claims.text: A process normally acts with the permissions of the user that started it, and the program does not pick that user; a few programs are set up to act as another user, and none used in this lesson is.
claims.source_hint: Linux man-pages, credentials(7) (user IDs inherited on execve) and execve(2) 'Set-user-ID and set-group-ID programs'

claims.text: Windows text tools traditionally end a line with a carriage return then a line feed, two bytes; Linux and macOS tools use a line feed alone, so a Windows line carries one byte more, and that byte stays attached to the last word of the line.
claims.source_hint: git docs on core.autocrlf / gitattributes eol (CRLF on Windows, LF elsewhere); ASCII control characters CR and LF

claims.text: Directory.GetCurrentDirectory() returns the current working directory of the application.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.IO.Directory.GetCurrentDirectory method

claims.text: AppContext.BaseDirectory gives the file path of the base directory of the application, which for this sample is the folder holding the built program files, and it is not the working directory.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.AppContext.BaseDirectory property (Summary and Remarks)

claims.text: Path.GetFullPath(string) resolves a relative path against the current working directory and returns an absolute path.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.IO.Path.GetFullPath(String) (Remarks on relative paths and the current directory)

claims.text: File.ReadAllText throws FileNotFoundException when no file exists at the given path, and UnauthorizedAccessException when the caller does not have the required permission for a file that does exist.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.IO.File.ReadAllText(String), Exceptions table (both rows)

claims.text: FileNotFoundException.FileName holds the path of the file that could not be found, in its fully resolved form rather than the relative path handed in.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.IO.FileNotFoundException.FileName property; run read-config-file from two folders and compare

claims.text: stat -c '%A %U:%G %n' prints the permission bits and file type in human-readable form, the owner name, the group name and the file name, in that order.
claims.source_hint: GNU coreutils manual, stat: format directives %A, %U, %G, %n

claims.text: chmod 600 on a file leaves read and write for the owner and removes every permission for the group and for others.
claims.source_hint: GNU coreutils manual, chmod: numeric modes; cross-check with the captured before/after strings -rw-r--r-- and -rw-------

claims.text: cd changes the working directory of the running script and pwd prints the working directory in force at that moment.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 Shell and Utilities, special built-in cd and utility pwd

claims.text: In the captured output of scripts/computer/permissions.sh at tag stage-0, the run reports the user root and the created file is owned by root:root.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: outputs/stage-0/scripts/computer/permissions.txt

claims.text: A bash script whose lines end with carriage return plus line feed breaks on Linux on a line whose first word the shell treats as the name of a program to run: the carriage return stays glued to that word, so the name reported is one character longer than the one typed.
claims.source_hint: GNU Bash manual, 3.1.1 Shell Operation and 2 Definitions: newline is the line terminator, so CR stays part of the token

claims.text: A process starts with the working directory of whatever started it, so a program run from a terminal starts with the folder that terminal was standing in.
claims.source_hint: Run dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- read-config-file from two different folders and compare the first printed line; Linux man-pages fork(2)/execve(2) on inherited attributes

claims.text: Path.GetFullPath and File.ReadAllText finish the same relative path against the same working directory, so the path GetFullPath prints is the path the open attempts.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.IO.Path.GetFullPath(String) Remarks; run read-config-file and compare the third printed line with the path in the not-found line

claims.text: On the stage-0 lab machine the script runs on, the run acts as the user root, to which that machine gives every permission, so the file's permissions do not stop this run from reading the file; the refusal happens to a run acting as an ordinary user.
claims.source_hint: Linux man-pages, capabilities(7) CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE; verify by executing scripts/computer/permissions.sh in the stage-0 lab box and by reading a mode-600 root-owned file as an ordinary user

claims.text: rm -rf removes a folder and everything in it, mkdir -p creates a folder, printf with > writes its output into a file, whoami prints the user name the process is running as, and cat prints the contents of a file.
claims.source_hint: GNU coreutils manual: rm (-r, -f), mkdir (-p), printf, whoami, cat; POSIX.1 Shell and Utilities on output redirection

claims.text: In bash, 2>&1 sends a command's error output to the same place as its normal output, and || runs the command after it only when the command before it fails.
claims.source_hint: GNU Bash manual, 3.6.4 Redirecting Standard Output and Standard Error, and 3.2.3 Lists of Commands (|| runs on non-zero exit status)

claims.text: The sample is registered as read-config-file in samples/DonHang.Samples/Program.cs at stage-0; dotnet run's --project argument is itself a relative path, so the command as written runs only from the repository's top folder, and from the project folder --project . is used instead.
claims.source_hint: .NET CLI reference, dotnet run --project option (path to the project file or its folder); examples/don-hang at stage-0: samples/DonHang.Samples/Program.cs sample dictionary

claims.text: In the string printed by stat -c '%A', the first character is the file type and the nine that follow are three groups of three — owner, group, others — each showing read, write and execute, with '-' where the permission is absent.
claims.source_hint: GNU coreutils manual, ls: 'What information is listed' (the file mode string) and stat directive %A

claims.text: Started from the top folder of the repository, the sample prints that folder as its working directory, then the folder holding the built program, then that first folder joined with app.conf, and then a not-found line carrying that same joined path.
claims.source_hint: Run dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- read-config-file from the top folder of examples/don-hang at stage-0 and read its four lines
